say.text: A 12-day-old is brought in because the lips and tongue look blue, worse when he cries. On auscultation there is a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left mid to upper sternal border, and you cannot make out a pulmonary component of S2.
What is your most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: An innocent flow murmur; he is just cold
Any cyanotic heart disease will do, I cannot pick one

say.text: Newborn murmurs are often innocent, so it is a tempting call. But blue lips with a harsh ejection murmur and an inaudible pulmonary S2 is not a flow murmur: the baby is cyanotic, so this is a cyanotic heart lesion.
Think about which cyanotic lesion is the commonest.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause here: cyanosis in a baby is never explained by cold alone. Look again at the murmur and S2 together.

say.text: Transposition is a fair thought because it is also a blue baby. But the question is which lesion is the most common cyanotic one, and the harsh ejection murmur points toward an outflow problem.
Have another look at the options.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember the exam angle: the 'most common cyanotic congenital heart disease' is TOF.

say.text: Blue baby plus a murmur means cyanotic congenital heart disease. Ask yourself which one is the **most common**, and then check whether a harsh ejection murmur with a missing pulmonary S2 fits it.
Yes, **Tetralogy of Fallot**. TOF is the **most common cyanotic congenital heart disease**, and the pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible, as you found.
The murmur is a **harsh systolic ejection** murmur, best heard at the left mid to upper sternal border.
Classic TOF has four components: a large, anteriorly malaligned **VSD**, an **overriding aorta**, **infundibular (sub-pulmonary) RVOT obstruction** and **right ventricular hypertrophy**.
We will rebuild these properly in the next part. For now, keep the case in mind.
Our baby is blue and has a murmur. Before I explain anything, make a guess.
Which single problem is most likely to make him blue?

choices.label: A narrowed outflow from the right ventricle
The VSD hole alone, whatever its size
Too much blood flooding the lungs

say.text: The murmur is an ejection murmur. Ask what blood would do if the way out to the lungs were tight, and the way out to the aorta were not.
The VSD is a real part of TOF, which makes it tempting. But the presentation varies with the severity of the **right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction**, not with the hole.
So what should you look at to explain how blue he is?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the obstruction sets how blue the child is.

say.text: Flooded lungs is the classic picture of other shunt lesions, so it is tempting. In TOF the opposite happens: with significant RVOT obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta and **bypasses the pulmonary bed**.
Now pick again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the reversal: in TOF blood bypasses the lungs.

say.text: Right. The presentation varies with how severe the **RVOT obstruction** is, and with significant obstruction most blood bypasses the lungs and goes toward the aorta.
That one idea is the thread for this whole module.
Last check before we start. A different baby with the same condition is brought to a clinic.
When does TOF most commonly present?

choices.label: As an acyanotic child with a murmur at school age

say.text: Our own case gave it away: think about how old the baby in the vignette was and what colour he was.
A school-age murmur is tempting, since many heart lesions are found that way. But TOF most commonly presents as a **cyanotic neonate**.
Now answer again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix this one: the usual first picture is a cyanotic neonate, as in our case.

say.text: Yes: **cyanotic neonate**. TOF is the **most common cyanotic congenital heart disease**, and it most commonly presents that way.
Next: the four parts of TOF, and which lesions are not among them.
